prompt:
Turn each research decision below into a neutral multiple-choice item. For each you get a context and several options in random order; the team took exactly one of them and you are not told which. Do not try to work out which.

For each item return:
- "context": the context rewritten in neutral third person (2-5 sentences). Keep its facts. Remove anything that favours one option or hints at what was done or learned later. Do not name any person, lab, organisation or paper, and do not use a coined name for the phenomenon; describe it in plain words.
- "question": one short line naming the decision, e.g. "Which evaluation should the team build?"
- "options": every option restated, keyed by its label, in ONE fixed form: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Frame ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no hedges; no digits (write numbers as words only if every option carries the same kind of number); no names. Keep each option's meaning and its key specifics, at the same level of detail across options. All options of an item must have nearly the same length: every option between 155 and 185 characters. Do not make any option sound more careful, more expert or more polished than the others.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "options": {"<label>": str}}]}

ITEMS:

=== key 58bf13fed636
Context: The paper reports that poisoned examples that have little effect alone can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. The regression model offered for this is only illustrative and does not explain every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly LoRA, with poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge.
O1: Make the headline a concrete, verified demonstration that a trait can be implanted from poison plus clean data, framed as a worst-case attack result and bounded to the tested models and setups.
O2: Organize the findings in a table that labels each one by evidence level and role (main finding, context-setting, speculation), so the strength of each claim is explicit.
O3: Framed the empirical result as the main contribution and listed limitations (small models, LoRA, constructed poison, lenient judge)
O4: Frame the finding as a general property of fine-tuning on confounded features, linking it to related known effects, and state it with its uncertainty about larger models and pretraining.
O5: Headline the result as a robust effect across paraphrases of the trigger and several poison types, and state clearly what the failed or absent cases show and do not show about absence elsewhere.

=== key c3089bd8f136
Context: In an experiment where a fine-tuned student was meant to adopt a 19th-century persona when prompted with a particular name, all rates were scored by an LLM judge using a two-label prompt closely adapted from earlier persona work. The judge was known to be lenient: it flagged responses with archaic fragments as positive. The team had to decide how to establish what the positive rates actually mean.
O1: Replace the judge-only score with a mechanical check, such as a rule-based match on persona-specific markers, and manually inspect the hits.
O2: Use the LLM judge over all transcripts, with a stricter prompt that requires a coherent persona, and report the stricter rates without any human audit.
O3: Report human and independent model-reader audits separately, with agreement stats against the automatic detector on sampled strata, rather than treating one grader as ground truth.
O4: Tighten the judge with a multi-criterion rubric (coherent persona, consistency, absence of mere archaisms) and validate it with counterfactual controls such as responses to unseen names, rather than relying on a human sample.
O5: Carried out a blind hand audit of 220 judge-positive responses plus a second strict rater

=== key 9cd98cf3c6d7
Context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings had left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents in context are mostly rejected. They now needed to decide how to probe whether any form of annotation could stop the implantation.
O1: Pick one annotation form (the strongest prefix/suffix variant) and study it in depth across many claims and models to isolate exactly what about it fails, rather than sweeping annotation types.
O2: Run a single matched ablation that varies one property of the warnings (for example, a fraction of documents carrying warnings) with a blind baseline lacking the warnings, and treat any prevention as an existence proof rather than a rate.
O3: Tested three interventions beyond simple prefix/suffix negations: repeated negations around every claim sentence, explicit corrections giving the true version, and local in-sentence negations.
O4: Hold the document set fixed and vary only where the false-flag appears and how it is phrased within otherwise identical documents, measuring belief with matched baselines and checking whether the model states the claim is false in its reasoning.

=== key d17768db573a
Context: The team measured belief in implanted fabricated claims after finetuning, using multiple-choice, open-ended, token-association, counter-question and pressure (robustness) evaluations. Counter-questions that ask the model to deny the true version, and robustness questions, already address whether the model merely parrots the claim, but they make up only a small share of the total question set. High overall belief rates could therefore still reflect increased salience of the claim rather than genuine belief.
O1: Added paired multiple-choice and lie-elicitation salience diagnostics, on top of counter-questions and robustness questions.
O2: Compare against a control model finetuned on documents that mention the claim with salient but clearly fictional framing, using it as a blind baseline to see how much of the belief score salience alone produces.
O3: Rely on the existing counter-question and robustness results, reporting them separately as the evidence for deep belief, without building additional salience diagnostics.
O4: Reweight the existing evaluation so that counter and pressure questions dominate the score, and report belief only on those items, with matched baselines on models finetuned on the claim in a non-believed framing.
O5: Test salience directly by measuring how often the finetuned model mentions the implanted fact in response to only distantly related questions, and whether it can self-identify which claim it was trained on, compared to a base model.

=== key 61062ce2aacb
Context: With local in-sentence negations (e.g., 'X is not a dentist'), the model trained on the Ed Sheeran claim scored 0% belief on all evaluations. The model trained on the Dentist claim showed 7% belief both before and after training; the residual came entirely from token-association questions rather than open-ended ones, where it correctly called the claim fabricated. The team had to decide how to interpret this leftover.
O1: Check for an artefact first by examining the token-association question wording and the judge's grading, and by comparing against an untrained model, before running any new training.
O2: Read a batch of the model's token-association transcripts and chain of thought to see whether it reasons about the claim being false, before deciding what the residual means.
O3: Check for a setup artefact by testing whether the token-association questions give a non-zero rate on a base model and on a control model trained on unrelated invented-character documents.
O4: Interpreted it as the Pink Elephant Paradox and tested this by masking loss on dentistry-related tokens, which removed the token-association vulnerability.
